articles.title_orig: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
articles.title_zh: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
articles.content_orig:
Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu .
Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly.
The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.”
A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection.
“Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said.
“They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested.
Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested.
Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine.
“They accuse Israel , tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly.
Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza.
The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views.
“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said.
“I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me.
“But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added.
Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera .
“I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year.
“There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
At the conclusion of Xi's visit, CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer if the leaders achieved anything new on artificial intelligence.
"I wouldn't say anything new," Greer said. I mean, we've established this this dialogue, AI dialogue with the Chinese, which really is when I think about it, I think of like the red phone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War. And the AI dialogue at a minimum is an opportunity, if the sides feel like they have something they need to share, whether it's risks or other things, we can do it. Most important thing is having a channel."
Greer said there would be "another meeting on AI in the next month or so" although the agenda has not yet been set.
Though Mr. Trump declined to answer shouted questions from reporters about Taiwan during Xi's visit, U.S. ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is "no change" in the United States' policy toward Taiwan.
" There's no change, no change in the Taiwan policy here," Perdue told CNBC Friday. "He's fully committed to the One China policy. We're committed to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiques, and the six assurances. Nothing has changed there. Of course, China has tried to coerce change in that regard. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there."
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.content_orig:
Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
Pope Leo has warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers of artificial intelligence at the start of a three-day visit to France.
“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Élysée.
At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco.
“Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.”
He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.”
Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of ​respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be ​bought and sold,” he said.
Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction ​of ​global leadership in ​recent months. He ​said ‌the world was “being ​ravaged ​by a handful of tyrants” last April.
The first official papal visit to France in 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024.
After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying , the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.”
A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde.
The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year.
Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”.
He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you ‘… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.”
Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals.
France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials.
In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram , near Lourdes.
On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar US media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.
Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Wisconsin police find dozens of partially clothed men in frat house basement in alleged hazing incident
articles.title_zh: Wisconsin police find dozens of partially clothed men in frat house basement in alleged hazing incident
articles.content_orig:
Two 20-year-olds were arrested after police were called to the scene of an alleged hazing incident where over two dozen young men were partially clothed and covered in liquids. Some of them were injured, police said.
The Madison Police Department said they received an anonymous tip about an event at the unaccredited Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity. When they arrived at the house, they found about 30 "partially clothed males covered in food, condiments and other liquids" in the basement. The room's thermostat was set to 81 degrees, police said.
Several of the men had "visible injuries consistent with being abused," police said.
The "vast majority" of the men were 18, police said.
A photo with the men's faces redacted shows the group in a dirty space with black walls and the Alpha Epsilon Pi letters painted on a piece of furniture.
Two people, identified by police as Brayden J. Klein and Samuel N. Vane, were arrested for hazing and disorderly conduct and taken to the Dane County Jail. The Madison Police Department said that the president and vice president of the fraternity were present and spoke to responding officers, but did not specify if Klein and Vane held those titles.
The men in the basement were escorted outside and checked for incapacitation and injuries.
"Several of these men had visible injuries consistent with being physically assaulted," police said.
No other charges have been announced in relation to the incident. An investigation remains ongoing, and those with information are asked to contact the Madison Police Department.
Alpha Epsilon Pi is an unrecognized and unaccredited student organization at the University of Wisconsin, police and the school said. It was suspended at the school in 2013 after a 17-year-old and another person were taken to detox after being served alcohol at a party hosted by the fraternity, the Associated Press reported, citing university records. The fraternity was terminated after a fourth incident involving either events, alcohol or both, and since 2016, there have been seven additional allegations related to intramural sports, disrespectful behavior, drinking and hazing.
The school said in a statement that because the chapter is still recognized by the national Alpha Epsilon Pi organization, it is legally allowed to operate as an unaffiliated fraternity chapter.
A spokesperson for the Alpha Epsilon Pi Headquarters said it takes the allegations concerning the Madison chapter "extremely seriously." The national organization plans to "cooperate fully" with the investigation, the spokesperson said, and members found responsible for criminal conduct will be expelled from the organization.
"Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for," the spokeperson said." There is no place for it in AEPi. No exceptions. No excuses. We educate our members about their responsibility to 'Be Your Brothers' Keeper.' This is not an optional value. It is a fundamental expectation of membership. Anyone who engages in hazing forfeits the privilege of being an AEPi brother."
The University of Wisconsin said it is also investigating the incident as it relates to its nonacademic misconduct process. Campus officials are providing support to affected students.
The Madison Police Department said that anyone whose safety is jeopardized during the Greek life recruitment process should contact authorities.

articles.title_orig: A nor’easter is strengthening near the East Coast. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.title_zh: A nor’easter is strengthening near the East Coast. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.content_orig:
Millions of Americans are gearing up for a rare, multiday nor’easter that is set to start pummeling the Northeast with rain, wind and flooding Friday.
Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people along the East Coast as of Friday morning, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island.
The storm already brought gusty winds and early flooding across the Eastern Seaboard on Thursday, with rough waves pounding shorelines. Winds up to 65 mph are forecast, with the strongest winds expected through Saturday night on Long Island in New York and in New England.
Heavy rain bands — up to 4 to 6 inches — will hit the area Saturday and into Sunday, and winds will push water onto shore, with 1 to 4 feet of inundation expected.
Widespread 1 to 3 inches of rain is possible from the Interstate 95 corridor to the coast. The Jersey Shore, Long Island and coastal New England are the locations likely to see the highest rain totals.
Waves of 10 to 18 feet are expected, with coastal flooding forecasts of 1 to 4 feet depending on the area.
The system is expected to intensify as it moves north. It will come onshore around New Jersey.
On Friday, the nor’easter will intensify as onshore winds increase from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, to Cape Cod, Massachusetts. By Saturday, rain will begin from the Jersey Shore to eastern Massachusetts and is expected to last all day.
Saturday will also feature the highest wind potential, with wind gusts that could reach 60 mph in coastal locations.
Rain will continue for the Northeast and New England on Sunday, as beaches continue to take a beating from the strong onshore winds.
The storm will still be spinning just off the coast Monday. While winds will be weaker, rain and beach erosion will continue.
Winds are expected to lead to travel delays and power outages into Monday.
Southeast New England faces the highest risk of power outages because of the strongest wind potential and top-heavy trees with leaves still on them.
Areas of New Jersey were already lashed by rough surf Friday morning, with videos showing waves crashing along the shore.
“The waves, the wave actions, the way it comes in, it just takes everything in its path,” said Mike Jones, the emergency management director for Upper Township, New Jersey. “And there’s really no way to stop Mother Nature.”
A full moon Saturday night is also expected to lift tides up to 5 to 6 inches.
One New Jersey resident told NBC News that to prepare for this weekend’s nor’easter, she closed up her whole house.
Outside Washington, abnormally high tides were seen along the Potomac River, inundating roads with floodwaters and leaving a popular Maryland music festival practically underwater. The first day of events was canceled in advance.
In North Carolina, winds greater than 50 mph have been recorded. A video showed a car in the state nearly swept into the ocean before a tow truck saved it.
Elsewhere in the region, emergency preparedness crews are cutting down trees and readying sandbags. Officials have warned of flooding in neighborhoods.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo is barreling toward Hawaii with 80 mph winds. It is a Category 1 storm and is moving north at 5 mph. At some point over the weekend, it is expected to become a major hurricane, upgraded to a Category 3 or 4.
The storm is forecast to stay south of Hawaii, but the islands will still feel Nolo’s wrath. Heavy rainfall — up to 30 inches on the Big Island — and intense winds are already affecting the state. People in Hawaii are preparing for the worst, expecting catastrophic flooding.
Just last month, Hurricane Lala brought destruction to Hawaii’s Big Island, damaging more than 100 homes and stranding people without water and power.
In addition to dangerous surf and damaging winds, mudslides are a major concern in Hawaii.
As of Thursday night, stores were sold out of generators and gas cans. Shops were boarded up and blocked with sandbags. Schools were let out Thursday to give residents more time to prepare for the storm’s effects.
Nolo is expected to reach full strength sometime Friday night.
Rebecca Cohen is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.
Sam Brock is an NBC News correspondent.
Ryan Chandler is a correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: 10-year Treasury yield hit a 19-year high—and some investors see opportunity to buy bonds
articles.title_zh: 10-year Treasury yield hit a 19-year high—and some investors see opportunity to buy bonds
articles.content_orig:
Often it doesn't feel like good news when a U.S. economic indicator matches a level last seen in 2007. But 10-year Treasury notes offering the highest yield since that year could be good news for investors looking to buy bonds.
Elevated inflation , especially higher oil prices, combined with expectations that the Federal Reserve will hike rates at least one more time this year, helped drive the 10-year Treasury yield to 5.208% on Thursday — the highest it's been since June 2007, before the global financial crisis. Yields remained elevated on Friday.
Higher long-term bond yields are often seen as a headwind for the stock market because they correlate with higher borrowing costs for consumers and companies, which can then slow down the overall economy. They can be especially bad news for consumers looking to take out a mortgage or other loan.
"As the 10-year yield goes up, borrowing costs for mortgages also go up almost in lockstep with it," says Dominic J. Pappalardo, chief multi-asset strategist at Morningstar Wealth. "Things like auto loans are also impacted. Really, kind of any consumer financing or borrowing rates are pretty closely linked to the 10-year Treasury yield."
On the flip side, rising Treasury yields do present an opportunity for bond investors.
"Higher interest rates benefit savers and investors just as much as they're harming spenders," Pappalardo says. "If you have money in savings or money to invest as interest rates go up, you are being paid a higher interest rate or generating more income from your savings and investments because of the yields moving up."
"Real yields" on Treasury notes, which measure yields after adjusting for expected inflation, have risen on net since February, around the time the war with Iran began and oil prices jumped. Investors can benefit from higher yields on longer-term bonds in particular, because they may be able to lock in higher rates for longer. Long-term Treasury yields are determined in the public bond market, which typically responds to higher inflation expectations, among other factors.
"Because of that, there's potentially a really strong opportunity to lock in very attractive levels," says Steve Laipply, global co-head of iShares Fixed Income ETFs for BlackRock. "We refer to it as a generational income opportunity."
Financial and investing professionals caution against making any major money moves based on short-term market conditions. Buying bonds because they look good right now may not be the best move for every investor. It's a good idea to work with a professional to see what makes sense for your individual financial situation.
Bond yields tend to rise when inflation expectations are high. Elevated oil prices due to the war with Iran have contributed to rising bond yields since February, and recent comments from the Fed have led investors to anticipate continued inflation and further rate hikes.
Treasury notes and bonds typically make fixed interest payments. When yields rise, prices of existing Treasurys tend to fall because their lower fixed payments become less attractive to investors compared with newly issued Treasurys. The inverse happens when yields fall.
Investors generally hold bonds to diversify their portfolios with assets that help them keep more of their money in a less volatile vehicle than stocks. Treasury notes and bonds also pay interest every six months, so they have an income benefit as well.
While individuals nearing or already in retirement could benefit most from elevated Treasury yields, Pappalardo says other investors with a near- to immediate-term goal, like those looking to buy a home in the next five to 10 years, may consider adding or increasing bond holdings.
Additionally, "investors should have an idea of their time horizon," Laipply says. "Do they want to invest for a period of five years, or are they comfortable investing longer-term, or do they simply want to stay very nimble?"
Though this week's acceleration in bond yields may be attractive to investors, they could continue to rise. If the Fed raises rates more than the hikes already priced in, or if oil prices move significantly higher, Treasury yields could rise even further, Laipply says.
On the other hand, if the conflict with Iran de-escalates and oil prices settle down soon, bond yields could fall. All to say, investors shouldn't try to time the bond market. However, there is less risk with Treasury yields compared with trying to time the stock market, Pappalardo says.
"Even if rates go from 5% to 6%, yeah, you may see some price decline, but it's relatively marginal," he says — although the impact may vary depending on a bond's duration, a measure of its sensitivity to interest rate changes.
Investors can buy individual bonds that are aligned with their time horizon or get broader exposure with a bond exchange-traded fund, Laipply says.
"Let's say you have an investor who's extremely cautious and wants to sort of wait to see how things settle down before they decide to commit by investing further out on the curve; they could buy something like SGOV," he says. That ETF includes Treasury bills with maturities of three months or less.
"There are a number of different ways for investors to earn income without feeling like they're taking risks that they're not comfortable with," he says.
But like the stock market, Pappalardo advises against investors making emotionally charged decisions on their investments. Though it can feel exciting to see the income potential with decades-high Treasury yields, "I wouldn't suggest somebody completely rebuilds their entire portfolio or investment approach today," he says.
"It's prudent and makes sense to tweak it to try and take advantage of that new marginal opportunity to generate more income off of bond investments," he adds. But "don't blow up everything and start from scratch."
Depending on your time horizon and risk tolerance, if 10% of your portfolio is currently in bonds, you may consider bumping that allocation up to 15% or 20%, he says, for example.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.
Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.
But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.
On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.
The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.
In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.
In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.
Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.
The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.
Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.
The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.
The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.
The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.
After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune .
Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.
In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.
Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.
Jane C. Timm is a senior reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Manchester City found guilty on almost all Premier League charges relating to financial breaches - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges the club has faced regarding breaching Premier League financial rules, according a report in The Athletic.
The sanctions have not yet been decided, and City are expected to appeal, according to an article by The Athletic’s David Ornstein on Friday, who cited anonymous sources briefed on the matter.
Sanctions could include points deductions, financial penalties, and even stripping titles won by City and relegation from the Premier League.
A spokesperson for City, who have denied the charges, said, “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.
“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”
Since a 2008 takeover by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family, City have been transformed from also-rans into the Premier League’s dominant force.
Eight of the club’s 10 league titles have come in the past 15 seasons, plus a first and only Champions League in 2023.
The club has been accused of breaching financial rules while on the rise to their current status.
Of the 115 charges, 80 are for breaches of regulations from 2009 to 2018, while the remaining 35 relate to failing to cooperate with the Premier League’s investigation.
The charges stem from leaked documents published by the German news magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.
Emails purportedly sent between top City executives showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from the UAE state-controlled airline Etihad and telecommunications firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group as income.
Other documents claimed to show off-the-books payments to then-manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
City have insisted there is a “comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence” to prove its innocence.
They have already defended their position in one case in which a two-year ban from the Champions League by UEFA was overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in 2020.
The CAS found most of the alleged breaches of overstating sponsorship revenue were either not established or “time-barred” because they fell outside the five-year statutory limit for prosecution.
But no such time limitation clause exists in the Premier League case.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.
A severe punishment would also raise doubts about the future of City’s cast of star players, including prolific striker Erling Haaland.
Other clubs could make a claim for titles to be stripped and compensation if City gained an unfair advantage by proscribed means.

articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran's next US concerts cancelled due to bad weather
articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday have been cancelled because of severe weather warnings in the area.
The singer had been scheduled to perform two shows at the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, near Boston, as part of his current US tour.
The tour has been in the headlines because of a row over a decision to drop Sheeran's support act Macklemore for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Stadium owners including the Gillette Stadium's Robert Kraft lobbied for his removal.
A statement from the venue said: "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium."
It added: "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.
"Refunds are available now at the point of purchase. Ticketholders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded."
Weather warnings for high winds are in force in the area until the early hours of Sunday, and officials have told drivers to minimise travel.
Sheeran was at the eye of a very different storm last week after the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour.
The decision came after the rapper made on-stage comments at earlier concerts including calling for "free Palestine" and referring to "genocide" in Gaza, as well as showing images of Gaza.
Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said Macklemore would not be allowed to appear at the Gillette Stadium, the home of his New England Patriots American football team.
Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by him. The promoter said venue owners including Kraft would have refused to let the concerts take place if Macklemore was on the bill.
Macklemore's removal from the tour led Sheeran's other support and backing artists to pull out in protest, and sparked a heated debate over free speech and the role of politics in music.
Returning to the stage last weekend, Sheeran told fans he "had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry".

articles.title_orig: Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at Prague Zoo, but curator warns "it's still a long run"
articles.title_zh: Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at Prague Zoo, but curator warns "it's still a long run"
articles.content_orig:
Five cheetah cubs had to survive a weather scare and the illness of their mother after their birth at the Prague Zoo. But they are doing well now, the zoo said on Friday.
The zoo said the quintuplets — four males and one female — that were born on June 18 had faced a tough time from the start.
Their mother, Daenerys, opted to give birth in an outdoor enclosure with a period of strong storms hitting Prague soon after.
Despite her inexperience, Daenerys took "exemplary" good care of her first cubs under such weather conditions, the zoo said .
Daenerys protected the five from torrential rains, licking water from their fluffy fur to keep them dry, curator Pavel Brandl said.
"Thanks to the mother's attentiveness, all five cubs survived the heavy downpours," the zoo wrote in a statement . "Soaking and subsequent pneumonia — along with predation — are common causes of mortality in cheetah cubs in the wild. It appears, however, that the mother dried her young by licking water from their fluffy coats with a characteristic dorsal mantle."
To make things worse, Daenerys suffered from an intestinal infection in August.
But despite all odds, the five looked lively and healthy on Friday.
"At this moment, everything seems fine, but it's still a long run," Brandl said. He said it might take a year before it's clear they will survive the crucial period after their birth.
"The mother of the cubs continues to surprise us," Brandl said after the cubs were born. "She arrived from France several years ago in poor physical and mental condition, and at the time, I was convinced we would never see offspring from this female."
Scientists say every cub is critical to saving the species, which is threatened with extinction.
Cheetahs, the fastest land animals in the world, can reach maximum speeds of between 70 and 75 mph. It's estimated that fewer than 7,000 of them remain in the wild.
Since 2020, the number of cheetahs in European zoos has declined by 25%, according to the zoo.
"Every successfully reared cub is therefore both an achievement and a source of hope," the zoo said.
Last October, 11 cheetah cubs were rescued from illegal trade in Somaliland in what a conservationist described as "one of the largest confiscations of the species."

articles.title_orig: Rep. Thomas Massie: Trump 'comeuppance' will happen on Election Day
articles.title_zh: Rep. Thomas Massie: Trump 'comeuppance' will happen on Election Day
articles.content_orig:
Seen on a screen below an exit sign, President Trump speaks on the first day of the 2026 Republican convention on Sept. 9 in Dallas. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption
There's a rare thing happening inside President Trump's Republican Party: dissent.
The president has long insisted on loyalty, but in recent weeks, a growing number of Republican candidates and elected officials have distanced themselves from core pieces of his agenda: from calling for an end to the U.S. war with Iran and relief from high prices, to criticizing his handling of key agenda issues like immigration.
It comes at a critical moment for the GOP. With less than 40 days until voting ends, the party is scrambling to hold onto a slim majority in Congress, where control of both the Senate and House of Representatives could come down to just a handful of toss-up races.
Trump's presence in the midterms looms large. He has repeatedly told voters to vote like he is on the ballot , despite facing historically low approval ratings . That could backfire, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll , which finds that a plurality of registered voters, 45%, and a majority of independents, view their vote as a vote against Trump.
"Trump's strength has always been primarily devised from his relationship to the voters," said Sarah Longwell, a GOP strategist and longtime critic of the president. "Republicans have always been loath to cross him because of his sort of stronghold on the party."
However, as Americans continue to sour on the president, Longwell argued that GOP lawmakers and candidates alike may "feel more comfortable bucking him on things that they really care about."
While most of the Republicans who have distanced themselves are on the ballot this fall, the splits have not been solely confined to the campaign trail.
On Tuesday, Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, who isn't up for reelection until 2030, released a letter urging the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate the president's son, Donald Trump Jr., after ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch financed large portions of a lavish party to celebrate his wedding.
Though past Trump-critics have largely been voted out of Congress or left the party, and the president still enjoys overwhelming support from Republican voters, Longwell sees Curtis' move as a potential indicator that lawmakers view the president's coalition as increasingly fragile.
"You are starting to see the very beginnings of people recognizing that Trump just doesn't have the juice that he once did and starting to push back."
In poll after poll, Americans consistently rank the cost of living as their top concern, and now, many say the conflict has added additional financial strain on their lives.
It's a connection that some Republican candidates running in toss-up races this cycle are acknowledging. On Monday, two GOP Senate candidates – Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Mike Rogers of Michigan – came out against the war and lobbied for additional relief for Americans impacted by rising costs.
"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," Hinson said in a statement on X , adding the conflict "needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."
The comments marked a shift for Hinson, who has previously voted against efforts to end the war .
In a video filmed at a supermarket, Rogers also made a point to link rising prices to the conflict.
"Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down. The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly. When it does, energy costs will plummet," he said.
Neither Hinson nor Rogers directly mentioned Trump in their statements, but their comments marked a clear break with the White House, given Trump has consistently defended his decision to go to war with Iran and has downplayed the conflict's effect on the economy.
There appears to be growing impatience with the war on Capitol Hill too. Just last week, seven House Republican lawmakers — up from four over the summer — joined Democrats in supporting a resolution aiming to remove U.S. forces from Iran.
"For a long time, Republicans have stuck with the president through thick and thin. But the ones who are facing real trouble at the polls need to differentiate themselves," said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and founder of the public affairs firm ROKK Solutions.
By choosing to cross Trump this late in the election cycle, Bonjean said it underscores how high the stakes are for Republicans.
"They're doing everything they can to make sure voters understand that they're much more independent than voting with Trump 100% or agreeing with him 100% of the time," he added.
That independence could prove crucial for Republicans whose political fate may be determined by some of the same key voting blocs that moved right two years ago and have since distanced from Trump, namely, Hispanic voters.
Even in red states like Texas and Florida, House districts with large Hispanic populations have seen drops in Republican support, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll .
That includes Florida's 27th district, where Rep. María Elvira Salazar is running to represent parts of Miami for a third term.
Last week, she released an ad directly criticizing Trump's immigration agenda, arguing his enforcement efforts have "gone too far."
"Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy," said Salazar, whose district is rated by the Cook Political Report as likely Republican. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
Like many Republicans, Salazar is still walking a fine line. In an interview with CBS News days after releasing her ad, she acknowledged having a "fantastic conversation," with Trump and described him as "very receptive."
"There are no attacks here," she added. "I'm just forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the South Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture."

articles.title_orig: From Sam Altman to Mark Zuckerberg: All the tech billionaires at the Trump-Xi dinner
articles.title_zh: From Sam Altman to Mark Zuckerberg: All the tech billionaires at the Trump-Xi dinner
articles.content_orig:
American tech billionaires filled the seats at President Trump’s flashy state dinner honoring Chinese leader Xi Jinping Thursday night, as concerns about the global AI race take center stage.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple Chairman Tim Cook, and AMD CEO Lisa Su were seen in photos at Trump and Xi’s table, at the very center of the festivities.
The invitees also included Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Alphabet’s Sergey Brin and Sundar Pichai, and Michael Dell of Dell Technologies.
In contrast to a 2015 dinner then-President Barack Obama hosted for Xi, no Chinese business leaders showed up, the Washington Post noted.
Still, the dinner marked a rare opportunity for the most powerful figures in tech to rub elbows with Chinese state dignitaries, as innovators have been divided in a heated debate over whether the world needs to slow development of dangerous AI models or push ahead.
President Trump has shrugged off doomsday warnings about AI’s potential to harm humanity, including one chilling prediction that it could lead to human extinction by 2030 – instead arguing that the more pressing threat is China pulling ahead in the race.
Chinese officials have also dismissed the warnings as “fear mongering” and “Cold War” tactics , urging companies to push ahead with development. Xi has stated that China will take the lead in fostering AI collaboration among developing countries.
Despite rising tensions within the industry, pols and tech figures were all smiles at the elaborate soirée in the East Room of the White House, walking a red carpet on the North Portico steps before the event.
The dinner featured red blossoms and red linens in a nod to the color of China’s flag, a toast of Schramsberg “Blanc De Noir,” and a menu with Chinese influences, all overseen by First Lady Melania Trump.
Notably absent from the dinner was Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, one of the industry leaders who has been most aggressive in calling for more stringent regulations on AI companies – drawing blowback from Trump himself.
Amodei recently published a lengthy essay proposing a three-step plan for global tech giants to slow their development of AI models, after an Anthropic researcher quit his job and sounded the alarm over potential dangers of the technology.
Altman and Musk – longtime rivals who were locked in a messy legal battle earlier this year – each backed Amodei’s proposal, which requires cooperation from regulators and tech companies around the world.
Trump accused Amodei of “pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’” and argued that any slowdown in US development could help China.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” the president wrote in a Truth Social post earlier this month.
Anthropic also butted heads with the government earlier this year when it refused to allow unfettered access to its technology for use in weaponry and mass surveillance.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered a blacklisting of the company, though a federal judge later struck down the ban.
Huang, who has been pushing to tap into the massive Chinese market, and Zuckerberg, whose company recently launched a popular AI agent , have each argued that the warnings around AI dangers have been blown out of proportion , saying the matter of development should be left to companies themselves – not regulators.

articles.title_orig: 2026 WNBA Playoffs Primer: Upsets, Chaos, and My Title Pick
articles.title_zh: 2026 WNBA Playoffs Primer: Upsets, Chaos, and My Title Pick
articles.content_orig:
The chaos of the final day of the WNBA regular season, which decided three of the four first-round playoff matchups, feels like a scaled-down harbinger of what’s next. We’re about to see an unusually wide-open first round; the gap between the no. 1 and no. 8 seeds is a historically tight seven games. For reference, that gap was 11 games last season and 17 the season before. Every lower seed boasts a little bit of a “nobody wants to see them in the first round” factor, besides the injury-plagued Dallas Wings, who carry the inferior but still scary “nothing to lose” label.
The WNBA’s 30th regular season has also been its longest, and the home-away-home format of the first round (which isn't organized by conference) will guarantee arduous travel for six of eight playoff teams. To boot, half the league is still getting over the jet lag and interruption caused by the FIBA tournament earlier this month in Berlin, held smack-dab in the final third of the WNBA season. There has never been a better time for an underdog to steal a game—or even a series.
I hesitate to romanticize the WNBA’s shoestring-budget past, but there’s something quaint about a season marked by exponential increases in player salaries hearkening back to the league’s adaptive, provisional roots. In time, the first round will be longer, and once expansion is complete, conferences will likely be reinstated as a structuring part of postseason play. But for now, in the messy middle of the WNBA’s ascendance , we are being given the gift of a rare first round where just about anything could happen—which has both its charms and frustrations.
With that in mind, let’s rank the first-round series based on the likelihood of an upset, starting with the longest shot, and examine the postseason race as a whole.
Paige Bueckers controls the ball against Gabby Williams
Dallas is the great afterthought of the postseason, and rightfully so. It has been absolutely decimated by injuries. Azzi Fudd, the 2026 no. 1 pick and the Wings’ best point-of-attack defender, is out for the rest of the season. The status of Alanna Smith, whose rim protection has carried a team to the WNBA Finals before, remains up in the air.
But they do have two wild cards:
I don’t see Dallas winning this series, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it kept up against the Valkyries’ style longer than expected.
One more stat: Dallas’s new starting lineup has the best offensive rating in the WNBA.
Breanna Stewart, Olivia Miles, and Han Xu go up for a rebound
When Sabrina Ionescu told reporters recently that New York isn’t your traditional eighth seed, she wasn’t just offering feigned optimism. The Liberty defeated the Lynx in five (controversial) games in the 2024 WNBA Finals, and the 26-18 record they clawed their way to this season—despite injuries to Ionescu, Satou Sabally (who is out for the year), Leonie Fiebich, and more—would have been good enough for the no. 5 seed last year.
The Lynx would have been a shoo-in to beat nearly any of the other lower seeds, but they've historically (and recently) struggled against New York's size.
As we found out in their last matchup, Fiebich and Breanna Stewart are one of the only duos with the size, speed, and versatility to switch an Olivia Miles–Napheesa Collier pick-and-roll.
With Collier back in the starting lineup, the Lynx are better as a whole than they were before her return—averaging a plus-18.5 net rating—but Collier adds some subtle wrinkles that could prove advantageous for New York. With Natasha Howard setting the bulk of Miles’s screens, the pick-and-roll had turned into a perpetual layup line for Minnesota. With Collier back, the Lynx have become more jumper-happy, partially because the two-time MVP runner-up gets double-teamed constantly. On its own, adding a little bit of variance to fuel a scintillating offense isn’t a bad thing. But the Lynx are also giving up five more points in the paint than they were before Collier’s return from her ankle surgeries. The five-time All-Star simply isn’t at 100 percent yet—by her own admission—and her gradual return to form has naturally taken a toll on Minnesota’s physicality in the paint, an area where it has to put forth a full-throttle effort to make up for its lack of defensive size.
One more stat: The Lynx are in the bottom three in the WNBA in points in the paint since Collier’s return .
Kiki Iriafen drives to the basket against Angel Reese
Hey, Washington: Get Angel Reese in foul trouble. She is frankly Atlanta’s only line of defense against the Mystics’ three-headed frontcourt monster of Kiki Iriafen, Shakira Austin, and Lauren Betts. The Dream are 7.9 points per 100 possessions worse defensively when Reese sits, and there’s a steep drop-off when her backups, even DeWanna Bonner, enter the game.
The Mystics and the Dream have similar styles. At a time when the rest of the WNBA is trending toward guard play and offense, both are in the top three in defensive rating, points in the paint, second-chance points, and free throw attempts. But in a war of attrition, the team with the most bodies—and, therefore, the most contingency plans—wins, and that’s the Mystics. For the Mystics, the youngest team in the WNBA, this is an opportunity to call shots, take names, form an identity, and prove that they are formidable as well as fun.
One more stat: The Mystics may be ranked 12th on offense, but they have the no. 1 free throw rate in the WNBA.

The Fever, meanwhile, await potentially devastating news on the status of Ty Harris, who had to be carried off the court in the final game of the regular season because of an ankle injury. Aliyah Boston also left that game early with a leg injury that has hampered her nearly all season long.
With Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell, Indiana has the best-scoring backcourt of all time. The Aces, on the other hand, have such putrid perimeter defense that Becky Hammon is starting essentially a one-way player in Stephanie Talbot, who has logged eight zero-point games this season. With Smith out, Hammon will likely have to go small around Wilson, exacerbating the Aces’ defensive issues. Per Synergy, nobody has given up more points as a primary defender this season than the Aces’ Jackie Young. Jewell Loyd, at 11th worst, is not far behind. The Fever have their own perimeter deficiencies on the defensive end, and I wouldn’t blame you for picking the team featuring the GOAT and the title pedigree to win here. But if the series turns into a defense-optional, offense-optimal free-for-all, I’m siding with Indiana, which has broken the 100-point mark this season more than any other team in WNBA history.

articles.title_orig: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.title_zh: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.content_orig:
One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.
In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".
"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

articles.title_orig: Block the Merger Coalition Asks Court to Reject Paramount’s Settlement With States Over Warner Bros. Deal
articles.title_zh: Block the Merger Coalition Asks Court to Reject Paramount’s Settlement With States Over Warner Bros. Deal
articles.content_orig:
A coalition of groups under the Block the Merger banner have filed an amicus brief – a third party representation in a court case – opposing the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.
The brief was filed late Thursday by Free Press, the Committee for the First Amendment, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Future Film Coalition and the International Documentary Association in the federal court of California.
Earlier that day Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, who is presiding over the case, gave interested parties permission to file amicus briefs with a deadline of 12:01 a.m. PT on Sept. 25 after the Block the Merger groups filed an emergency motion requesting leave to file. The legal move came after 12 state attorneys general reached a settlement over proposed legal action over the merger.
“Since the terms of the consent decree were announced on Monday morning, few outside of those with a financial interest in this deal have suggested that it addresses the harms to competition, creativity, and independent journalism this merger will cause for years to come. The deal has been met with silence, skepticism, or tepid support at best,” the groups said in a joint statement.
“The arguments laid out in this brief reflect the concerns that just days ago, California Attorney General Bonta also willingly voiced. While we may never know what caused the radical turnabout to deliver such a toothless settlement, we do know that this consent decree bucks governmental safeguards designed to protect the public from harm. The court should reject it outright.”
The League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) has also filed an amicus brief against the settlement.

articles.title_orig: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.title_zh: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.content_orig:
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.
In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.
It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday , European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.
Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.
However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

articles.content_orig:
Fox News Digital spoke to Donalds about his tightening race for Florida governor against Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican.
Florida gubernatorial candidate, Republican Congressman Byron Donalds , is taking aim at his Democratic opponent David Jolly over his shifting political positions and party affiliation, in a contest that is resurfacing themes from the 2016 congressional race between Jolly and Charlie Crist.
"You were pro-choice, then you were pro-life, then you were pro-choice. It was only after you switched parties that you switched your position. This was not a matter of conviction for you; it was for political convenience," Jolly said about Charlie Crist when Jolly was a Republican running against Crist, a Democrat, for Congress in 2016.
Ten years later, Jolly is now a Democrat running for Florida governor and facing the same criticism for allegedly changing his positions for political gain, this time, in his race for governor against Donalds.
"The shift in positions by David Jolly is not because of personal conviction, it is purely because of political convenience," Donalds told Fox News Digital, referencing that 2016 exchange.
DESANTIS ENDORSES FLORIDA GOP SLATE INCLUDING BYRON DONALDS IN GOVERNOR'S RACE
Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., takes aim at gubernatorial opponent David Jolly's decades-long history of changing parties and political positions in an interview with Fox News Digital. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images ; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Some of the shifts in Jolly’s positions include issues like abortion, immigration and drilling off the coast of Florida.
As a Republican, Jolly said he believed "life begins at conception," authored legislation to defund Planned Parenthood and co-sponsored fetal-personhood legislation. He also voted for a federal 20-week abortion ban. Now running as a Democrat, Jolly calls himself "pro-choice," supports codifying the Roe v. Wade framework and says he would veto legislation restricting abortion access as governor.
Jolly’s immigration views have also shifted sharply as he attempts to run for governor in a state that voted for Trump each of the last three presidential cycles by wide margins, with many voters motivated by Trump’s immigration policies.
As a Republican, he campaigned on securing the border, supported tighter screening for Syrian and Iraqi refugees and voted for the American SAFE Act. Today, he says the country should have "wide gates" for people coming to work or seek asylum, argues that crossing the border without legal status should not necessarily be treated as a crime in those circumstances and has called the Republican link between immigration and crime "gross," "immoral" and "wrong."
As voters consistently say that affordability is a top-of-mind concern, Donalds is also hitting Jolly’s record on healthcare as an example of inconsistency that shows a lack of credibility on the issue.
NEVER-TRUMP REPUBLICAN IS TOP DEM CHOICE IN CRUCIAL FLORIDA PRIMARY
Former Republican Representative David Jolly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate for Florida, speaks during the National Action Network (NAN) 35th Anniversary Convention in New York on Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"When David Jolly was in Congress, he opposed Obamacare," Donalds said. "Now trying to run for governor, he wants to expand Obamacare in Florida. I mean, these are just some of the complete shifts that we've seen in what he stands for."
Another issue Donalds is taking issue with involves the period after the devastating Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which sent oil and tar balls washing ashore along roughly 178 miles of Florida coastline, contributed to an estimated loss of 1.88 million planned recreational visits in northwest Florida and cost the region $1.3 billion in visitor spending, $2.04 billion in economic output and more than 20,000 job-years.
Within a year of the spill, Jolly’s lobbying firm represented a client that publicly advocated for legislation that could have expanded offshore drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Three Bridges Advisors listed H.R. 909, the Roadmap for America’s Energy Future, among the subjects of its 2011 lobbying activity for the Free Enterprise Nation, which supported the bill. Jolly also wrote a post on the group’s website stating that Free Enterprise Nation was "advocating for" the legislation.
BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY'
Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican from Florida and gubernatorial candidate, won Florida's Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Orlando, Fla., easily fending off challengers after receiving an early endorsement from President Donald Trump. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Jolly said he had "never lobbied for offshore drilling," but PolitiFact rated that claim "Mostly False" after finding that Jolly acknowledged attending a meeting where the bill was discussed, which lobbying experts said technically counted as lobbying.
Donalds cited the controversy to Fox News Digital saying, "Deepwater Horizon exploded in the Gulf of America, David Jolly went and became a lobbyist for more oil drilling off the coast of Florida, that is a fact and so, what we're seeing is a history of somebody who does everything possible, will say whatever, will be paid by whomever that are only in the interest of David Jolly."
With polls showing a tightening race, the RealClearPolitics average gives Donalds a nearly 4-point lead. The candidates are also sparring over debate scheduling: Donalds has agreed to three proposed debates, while Jolly, who previously accepted two other debate invitations, has now ruled out participating in debates this cycle.
"Now he's ducking debates," Donalds told Fox News Digital. "He won't debate me because he knows that on a debate stage, I will hold him accountable for these things."

Jolly has hit Donalds on the campaign trail on a variety of issues as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida since Lawton Chiles won re-election in 1994. Primarily, Jolly has focused on data centers and labeled Donalds as a candidate more interested in partisan culture-war battles than addressing Florida’s rising housing, insurance and healthcare costs.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Jolly campaign for comment.
Donalds told Fox News Digital that Jolly’s flips on both party registration and the issues are things his campaign will continue to focus on.
"What you find with David Jolly is somebody who's done a complete 180 simply to run for office again and to gain relevance again and the people of Florida simply cannot trust David Jolly because we cannot afford David Jolly’s flip-flopping when it comes to the great state of Florida," Donalds said.

articles.title_orig: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.title_zh: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.content_orig:
Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack," according to Reuters .
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.
