“This move is a diplomatic all-timer,” Santi Ruiz, a policy-focused writer for the Institute for Progress and editorial team member at AI company Anthropic, posted on X. “It's like Messi cutting inside. You know it’s coming. It doesn’t matter how many times they run it. You’re getting those pandas, and you’ll like it.”
The tried-and-tested offering came once again on Thursday as Chinese President Xi Jinping announced during his state visit to the U.S. that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang , two giant pandas from a research base in Chengdu, would be lent to Zoo Atlanta in the state of Georgia—but whether this so-called panda diplomacy remains as welcome as it has over the decades is less clear, eliciting mixed reactions in 2026.
The practice gained traction after the National Zoo received giant pandas from Beijing in the wake of President Richard Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon’s historic trip to China in 1972, which marked a new, positive chapter in U.S.-China relations.
China claims ownership of nearly all the giant pandas in the world, even their offspring, and controls who receives them. Beijing eventually shifted from gifting giant pandas to leasing them to other countries in 1984 as the animal’s population dwindled, but the practice continued and spread to other nations like Austria, Canada, and Malaysia. China regularly considers loaning pandas an act of goodwill—even when the host nation typically foots the bill of about $1 million annually for a pair.
A giant panda’s presence or absence in a country tends to represent ebbs and flows of its relationship with China. For instance, amid tensions with Japan over Taiwan , Tokyo returned two giant pandas to Sichuan on loan in January, marking the first time Japan does not have a giant panda since 1972, when China-Japan ties first normalized. In 2010, two U.S.-born panda cubs returned to China , days after Chinese officials warned then-President Barack Obama against meeting the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing considers a separatist.
“No other animal has been turned into a symbol to the extent that pandas have been,” says Czeslaw Tubilewicz, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University.
It’s also no coincidence that Zoo Atlanta received the giant pandas, Tubilewicz says, as the gift represented Beijing’s appreciation of Georgia’s historical economic partnership with China on several aspects: “When most southern states, especially Republican states, turned very negative on China, Georgia continued its pro-China policy consistently. So when it comes to those pandas, and in [Zoo Atlanta], in a way, Xi Jinping is trying to kill two birds with two pandas.”
But China’s transformation from a developing economy to one of the world’s superpowers has also raised questions about whether the gesture of sending giant pandas still works. China is massively different from how it used to be in the 1970s, and is currently embroiled in a wide range of issues, not only with the U.S., but also with other countries, which makes categorizing it neatly as a friend or foe less easy.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, tells TIME that “the image of the pandas as soft, friendly, and cuddly—they don’t work today because a lot of [China’s aggressive] actions now are a lot more visible and fresh in people’s minds.”
“No one cares about pandas when national security or geostrategic interests come into play,” Tubilewicz added.
A 2022 peer-reviewed study at the University of Connecticut found that U.S. students who viewed panda videos that were not sourced from the government were likely to have a positive attitude toward Chinese culture and, in turn, Chinese people.
But while China’s practice of leasing pandas gives some people warm feelings, it makes others hot with anger. Conservationists and animal advocates have argued against using pandas as geopolitical pawns. Following the South Korea-China Summit earlier this year, the countries’ respective environmental officials discussed additional giant panda loans. But a Korean animal rights group slammed the move , saying that the creatures “are not beings born for human entertainment or interstate friendship.”
And many others are also starting to look past the panda diplomacy and demand other measures. A 2026 survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 28% of respondents said sending pandas to American zoos would improve their view of China, but much higher percentages said that more concrete actions like Chinese cooperation on curbing fentanyl precursors or easing trade restrictions would improve their view of China.
“The symbolism was still dominant in the 1970s,” Chong said. “It’s just that, given the lack of information, given the environment of that time, the symbolism probably got a lot more traction before than today.”
While surveys show many Americans are warming to China , Chong says “deep reservoirs of reservations remain,” particularly among Trump’s MAGA base: a July survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says that 63% of MAGA Republicans favor limiting the growth of Chinese power.
“Affection for pandas does not automatically translate into support for Chinese government policies,” Yu Tao, associate professor in Chinese Studies at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “Its more realistic contribution is to sustain public goodwill and opportunities for cooperation. The strongest case for panda diplomacy is that it gives people something they want to preserve in a relationship otherwise defined pretty much by disputes.”

World number one ‌Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the China Open, saying ⁠that he is ⁠not yet ready to compete as he continues to recover from the knee injury that also forced him to miss the ⁠US Open.
The 25-year-old Italian has not played since capturing his fifth major title at Wimbledon in July.
Sinner skipped the Canadian Open and withdrew from ⁠the Cincinnati Open, two key hard-court tune-up events, before also pulling out of the US Open.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

articles.content_orig:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered non-sensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. Negotiations under the new U.S.-China "Board of Trade" mechanism are focused on "pure trade issues," Greer said, rather than U.S. national security restrictions on advanced technology.
"All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer said.
Trump and Xi, after they met in Beijing in May, announced the establishment of the "Board of Trade" to manage trade between the two rivals in non-sensitive products. Businesses have been waiting for more details on what categories of trade would be set aside, under the new framework, for lower tariffs.

'Pink clouding', sometimes called Pink Cloud Syndrome, describes a period of intense optimism or euphoria that can occur early in addiction recovery before the realities and difficulties of recovery set back in.
The expression can also be used more broadly to describe a temporary euphoric state or the feeling that everything is suddenly rosy.
In the chorus, she sings: 'Cause I was pink clouding from the thrill of it (Pink) / Skydiving as you wrapped your arms around my body / Gray rocking where the arrow hit (Gray) / Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry / I didn't want to let you down (Pink cloud, pink cloud) / So I left you up there on a pink cloud (Pink, pink cloud).'

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Indexes Tick Higher at Open as Treasury Yields, Oil Prices Pull Back; Nasdaq, S&P 500 on Pace for Weekly Gains
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Indexes Tick Higher at Open as Treasury Yields, Oil Prices Pull Back; Nasdaq, S&P 500 on Pace for Weekly Gains
articles.content_orig:
The bond market is yelling at the Federal Reserve, but the messages are coming from different directions and pose a dilemma for policymakers as they seek to strike a balance that won't tank the economy.
Treasury yields continued their upward march Thursday as investors sought to price in a variety of factors: inflation still hovering well above the Fed's 2% goal, another bump up in energy prices and the impact of a global hyperscaler financial arms race and accompanying debt issuance.
In the past, policymakers have been willing to look through inflation spurts from temporary shocks like high energy prices and tariffs. And the narrative not so long ago was that the artificial intelligence investing boom was a story that would last a year or two and ultimately prove disinflationary.
But now Fed officials are rethinking the impact of those factors and seeing the danger of more durable inflation.
At the same time, markets are grappling with a central bank that suddenly has no interest in telegraphing its next moves, leaving an uncertain calculus on who is calling the shots — policymakers or market players.
"The time of looking through the initial supply shock has come to an end," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "The bias has to be towards restoring price stability, and they should take what's going on seriously."
Markets expect the central bank will indeed take a firmer hand on inflation.
Over the past day or so, traders raised the odds of a rate hike in October, which would come only a month or so after last week's quarter percentage point increase . They also see a third increase either late this year or early in 2027, with additional hikes possible in subsequent months.
That's a big switch from a Fed that in June projected it might hike once this year and then be done before starting to cut in the next couple of years.
"My view coming out of the [September] meeting was that we're going to get three rate hikes," Brusuelas said. But modeling performed at his firm about the potential for higher yields, along with a prolonged cycle of AI investment, changed that view.
The modeling indicated that sharply higher long-term yields could slow growth and increase unemployment and still not get inflation back to 2%. RSM found that even a 5.5% 10-year yield — it was around 5.15% on Thursday — would lower growth to 1.5% and lift unemployment to 4.7% while core inflation remained stuck at 2.4%.
"The Fed is underestimating what's going to be necessary to restore price stability — that we're probably not talking two or three hikes. We're talking five or six," Brusuelas said.
Not everyone on Wall Street agrees. Some strategists think the market is getting ahead of itself — that yields now essentially are pricing in stronger economic growth and are overly sensitive to the vagaries of oil prices amid the ongoing tensions in the Middle East.
"The rise in yields has not been due to expectations of a too-dovish Fed allowing inflation to persistently exceed target. Instead, the rise has been in real yields as investors priced-in the Fed setting higher policy rates," Citigroup economist Andrew Hollenhorst said in a note. "It should not be surprising that this has led to both higher shorter-term and longer-term yields."
Indeed, several key Fed officials, while endorsing near-term rate hikes, also are counseling patience.
New York Fed President John Williams , whose position puts him in the vice chair slot of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, said Thursday that it's "reasonable" to expect another hike by the end of the year, but also noted that officials need to keep watching the data before getting on a pre-set "forward guidance" track of locking in rate hikes.
Similarly, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson also indicated additional policy tightening is likely but characterized the potential moves as "modest," hardly an indication that she thinks a string of hikes is likely.
Still, the Fed faces a policy crossroads: Tighten too much and risk cutting off the expansion, or tighten too little and risk losing the market's faith that it is sufficiently tuned into inflation risks.
"Weak guidance guardrails risk putting ... central banks in a position where they may have to decide between a sub-optimal hike and disappointing the market and risking hard-won credibility," Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI, said in a note. "Lack of guidance also means whatever decision they take risks generating an outsized market response — either substantially further tightening or easing market rates."
Guha is in the camp that the market's expectations are "too aggressive" while also seeing the Fed's dilemma.
"Delivering back-to-back hikes — particularly without forward guidance as to how to interpret them — would risk sending a very hawkish signal that would reprice the rates curve further and to an unpredictable extent," Guha said. "But, skipping a hike priced odds-on in the market could also lead to a large repricing in the other dovish direction."
The conflict is critical now because Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has emphasized letting markets help guide policy. That's a big reversal from central bank policy since the global financial crisis in 2008, when the Fed used its forward-guidance tool to signal to investors which way rates were headed.
"His framework appears significantly less rooted in economic measurement details and significantly more reflective of market narratives," UBS economist Jonathan Pingle wrote of Warsh. "No Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve has emphasized considering the signals from financial markets as an input into monetary policy decisions as strongly as Chairman Warsh."
With a yield surge that has taken the 30-year bond to its highest level since 2004, market dynamics have swung Warsh from someone calling for cuts prior to taking the job in May, to a chair who seems to have forged a hawkish coalition on the FOMC.
In fact, Pingle speculated that Warsh, following last week's post-meeting news conference, "left little doubt to us that his views more closely align" with Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, arguably one of the most hawkish of this year's voting group, "than anyone else on the FOMC."
For now, at least, markets are going with the interpretation that Warsh will let the Treasury market guide him toward progressively higher benchmark rates.
"There's a good reason why central bankers are beginning to be concerned about overheating in the investment section of the economy," said Brusuelas, the RSM economist. "Mr. Market is signaling something to policymakers like Kevin Warsh that they ought to listen to."

iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes.
Apple Wallet offers a host of features to help you replace your physical wallet and keys.
It holds credit cards, driver’s licenses, transit cards, boarding passes, event tickets, car keys, home keys, hotel keys, and more.
And with iOS 27, the Wallet app takes another big step toward being the only wallet you need.
That’s because you can now import physical passes, tickets, membership cards, and the like into Apple Wallet.
Here’s how it works, per Apple :
iPhone and Apple Watch users will be able to create and store passes in Apple Wallet from physical cards, like loyalty or membership cards, eliminating the need to fumble through pockets and bags. With Siri mode in the Camera app, users simply point their iPhone at any physical card with a barcode or even screenshot a digital one, and they’ll be prompted to save it to Apple Wallet. Users can also create and add a pass directly from Apple Wallet. Once added, passes are ready to present as a barcode or QR code right from their iPhone or Apple Watch.
Digital passes are a lot more common today than when Apple Wallet first launched. But they aren’t available for everything.
I definitely still encounter businesses and events that utilize physical passes exclusively. And when I do, it adds a little anxiety to my life because I then need to remember to bring those passes with me at the right time.
But with iOS 27, everything can start going in the Wallet app, which is always with me. By putting everything in Wallet, the mental burden of remembering to bring something extra is suddenly gone.
Are there any physical passes you’ve added to Apple Wallet in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Winners and losers from Packers' Thursday Night Football dud vs. Falcons
articles.title_zh: Winners and losers from Packers' Thursday Night Football dud vs. Falcons
articles.content_orig:
The Atlanta Falcons played like a rejuvenated team that finally had its quarterback back . The Green Bay Packers had the look of an undermanned squad still asking too much of its own quarterback.
That pretty much summed up an ugly Thursday night game in Wisconsin, the Falcons steamrolling the Packers 35-14 for their first win of the season as QB Michael Penix Jr. made his 2026 debut. Atlanta, which had 16 points all season entering the game, rolled off 27 in a row at one point in a runaway that immediately restored them to relevance in the NFC South. The Pack, meanwhile − still without injured superstar OLB Micah Parsons and Pro Bowl RB Josh Jacobs, among others − moved into the basement of the NFC North with a 1-2 record that somehow seems far more problematic than Atlanta’s.
The scoreboard said plenty, but there were quite a few other winners and losers Thursday, and they are as follows:
The Falcons quarterback, and team’s highly scrutinized first-round pick from 2024, started his first game in nearly a year after sufficiently recovering from the third ACL reconstruction of his football career, dating back to his college days. He threw an interception while getting reacclimated on his first drive, but ultimately completed 18 of 25 throws for 256 yards and a TD. His connection with WR Drake London certainly seemed fully intact, the duo hooking up nine times for 194 yards. Playing on a Thursday night also confers another benefit to Penix, who now gets 11 days to recover and gauge how his body responds with Atlanta scheduled to next play Oct. 5 in New Orleans, Week 4’s Monday nighter.
In the depths of their 0-2 start , the Falcons entered the game with nary a touchdown in the previous seven quarters – and just one all season – and had not played a snap in the opposition red-zone in 2026, a dry spell no team had experienced through its first two games since 2008. Thursday, they scored four touchdowns in five visits inside Green Bay's 20-yard line.
Y’all remember he’s a two-time NFL Coach of the Year, right? That seems to get obscured a bit after the rocky end to his six-year tenure with the Cleveland Browns – where all tenures end rockily – and was certainly accentuated by Atlanta’s ghastly start to this season. But if Penix didn’t completely unlock Stefanski’s offense, which did rack up a gaudy 498 yards, he certainly stabilized it and provided ample hope that the Falcons could still be a contender for the divisional throne this season. After notching his first win as Atlanta's HC, Stefanski is also now 6-0 on Thursday nights … 41-60 (playoffs included) during the rest of the week.
Maybe the lone silver lining for the Green and Gold, the fifth-year receiver continues to show what he's capable of when healthy, which has been the biggest obstacle to date during his career. Watson's first-quarter TD catch, which staked Green Bay to an early lead, was his fourth of the season, tying him for the league lead − albeit with one more game under his belt than Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Detroit's Amon-Ra St. Brown.
It's been a rough year-plus for the Atlanta defensive coordinator, even more so off the field than on. In 2025, Ulbrich's son infamously prank-called then-Colorado QB Shedeur Sanders as he tumbled into the third day of the draft, embarrassing the family and lightening the coach's wallet. This year has been much worse, Ulbrich's wife losing her battle with cancer in July. An inspired defensive effort against the Packers − and with the Falcons down several key starters due to injuries and pass rusher James Pearce Jr.'s suspension − only counts for so much, but it's nice to see something go right for the NFL lifer given all he's been through on a personal level.
As you’d expect, Bijan Robinson provided plenty of mustard to the Falcons offense, rushing for 194 yards and two scores. However he also got some nice backup from RB2 Brian Robinson Jr. (no relation), who chipped in with 50 yards and a score of his own.
Boy, do the Packers miss Jacobs – to say nothing of the legitimacy he provides to the play-action approach coach Matt LaFleur favored in 2025, a strategy that was obviously dead in the water against Atlanta ... yet curiously employed on fourth-and-1 from the Falcons' 7-yard line on the Packers' first possession of the second half. (The play failed miserably.) After averaging a meager 64.5 yards on the ground in their first two games, the Pack were far more ineffectual Thursday – producing all of 17 yards, among the lowest totals in the storied franchise's history. And with no return in sight for Jacobs, who remains on the commissioner’s exempt list – not to mention a battered O-line that was missing LG Aaron Banks and RT Zach Bako-Bewele, who’s out for the season with a knee injury – little reason to believe matters will improve any time soon.
The leader of the Pack on the field and at the bank – with a contract averaging $55 million annually – Love understandably continues to struggle trying to operate an offense that’s completely out of kilter while attempting to compensate for a defense that’s been grated for at least 35 points twice in three weeks. Aside from the lopsided pass-run ratio (54 dropbacks vs. nine rushes on Thursday), Love was also navigating his new blocking combination without injured WR Jayden Reed. While his position and paycheck put the onus on him, Love, who’s barely completing 50% of his passes this season − despite 312 empty-calorie yards and two TDs through the air Thursday − continues to be stuck in what’s presently a very unenviable position.
"I think a lot of areas we need to improve. But at the end of the day, I'll just sit here and look at myself and say there's so much stuff I can improve on to make us as an offense better," Love said afterward. "It always starts with me. To be the leader of the team, I've got to improve and be better in a lot of areas. There's a lot of stuff that I'll look at on film that I won't be happy with how I performed tonight."
There shouldn't be too much blame assessed to the Packers pass rusher. But we can't ignore that his roughing penalty on Penix late in the first quarter − when the Packers were leading 7-0 − kept the Falcons on the field following what appeared to be a failed third down. Bijan Robinson escaped for a 55-yard run on the next play, was in the end zone two snaps later, and the Falcons never looked back. Oops.
If you took the Falcons' Kyle Pitts or Packers' Tucker Kraft with an early pick in your fantasy draft ... bummer. They've combined for 11 receptions, none for TDs ... all season.
Unless Penix gets reinjured − sadly, his history suggests it will happen − the Dolphins castoff ain't playing extensively here. Expected to start in Week 1 before he injured an oblique muscle in practice , Tagovailoa's best bet to rekindle his career in 2026 might entail a release from his one-year deal or a trade to a quarterback-needy team, say the New York Giants potentially?
Arguably the most iconic stadium in the NFL , it’s been privy to a lot of good football in recent decades – and most certainly on opening night. But not Thursday. The loss to the previously winless and inept Falcons was not only embarrassing and frustrating for the locals, it also ended the Packers’ streak of winning 13 consecutive home openers.

articles.title_orig: Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were false
articles.title_zh: Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were false
articles.content_orig:
Unnamed woman who filed and later dropped lawsuit against rap superstar states that she never met him, contrary to initial allegation of 2000 assault
A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 years old has formally withdrawn her allegation, saying that she has never met the rap superstar.
The unnamed woman had originally made the allegation in a lawsuit filed in 2024, claiming that Jay-Z , real name Shawn Carter, had drugged and raped her with Sean Combs, known as P Diddy. The incident was alleged to have happened at a party after an MTV awards ceremony in 2000.
Jay-Z denied the allegations, describing them as a blackmail attempt, and Combs also denied them. Jay-Z’s lawyer maintained the events relied on an “impossible timeline”. The woman dropped the lawsuit in 2025 , and Jay-Z filed a counter suit .
As that lawsuit progresses, the woman has now said her claims were false. “Shawn ‘Jay-Z’ Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr Carter. Mr Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever,” she said in a declaration obtained by Rolling Stone .
She added that there was “no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter. I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone.”
The woman has now been dropped from Jay-Z’s lawsuit, though the rapper is still pursuing her former lawyers, claiming they should have known the allegations were “contradicted by publicly available information, internally inconsistent, and unsupported by any credible story or investigation”. Earlier this month, as they made a motion to have the lawsuit dismissed, lawyer Tony Buzbee and his co-counsel described it as “a malicious prosecution”.
Regarding the woman’s new statement, Buzbee told Rolling Stone: “If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that’s new information.”
The woman’s current lawyer, James Blair Newman Jr, said: “Our client maintains that she was a victim of sexual assault, but she was entirely mistaken in her allegations identifying Mr Carter.”
Continuing her statement, the woman said memories of sexual assault were triggered by seeing an advertisement calling for victims of Combs to come forward. Combs was being investigated for a number of alleged sexual assaults, and – unrelated to the unnamed woman’s case – was eventually found guilty on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution, receiving a four year and two month sentence in October 2025.
The woman said that after making the allegations, she was unaware of the lawsuit being filed on her behalf and, after she expressed doubts about her claims, the lawsuit was dropped.
Jay-Z has previously spoken about the impact the allegations had on his life. When the case was dropped, he said: “The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed,” and speaking to GQ in March he said: “I haven’t been that angry in a long time, uncontrollable anger. You don’t put that on someone – that’s a thing that you better be super sure [about].”
He said he had refused to settle the lawsuit out of court: “ I can’t take a settlement – it ain’t in my DNA … I would die .”

articles.title_orig: Details on U.S.-China trade negotiations coming Monday, USTR Greer says
articles.title_zh: Details on U.S.-China trade negotiations coming Monday, USTR Greer says
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered non-sensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. Negotiations under the new U.S.-China "Board of Trade" mechanism are focused on "pure trade issues," Greer said, rather than U.S. national security restrictions on advanced technology.
"All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer said.
Trump and Xi, after they met in Beijing in May, announced the establishment of the "Board of Trade" to manage trade between the two rivals in non-sensitive products. Businesses have been waiting for more details on what categories of trade would be set aside, under the new framework, for lower tariffs.
The news come as Washington and Beijing have also agreed to extend their broader trade truce by two months, giving the two sides more time to negotiate over longstanding economic disputes.
Greer said Friday that the U.S. views those two months as "compliance periods" to assess whether China is following through on earlier commitments, including purchases of U.S. soybeans and other agricultural products and access to rare earths needed by American manufacturers.
"Whenever we have these compliance periods that roll over, it's a time for us to assess, reassess and determine whether or not to continue this period of relative peace on the economic front with the Chinese," Greer said.
Meanwhile, tariffs have sharply altered U.S. trade flows . Greer said Friday that the U.S. goods trade deficit with China has fallen nearly 40%, while acknowledging that some trade has shifted to other countries as companies adjust their supply chains.
Mexico has been one beneficiary of that shift. U.S. imports from Mexico reached a record $60.6 billion in July, according to the Census Bureau . The seasonally adjusted U.S. goods deficit with Mexico increased by $7.2 billion that month to $27.5 billion, according to the Census Bureau.
"When you impose tariffs ... you see market actors starting to do what market actors do, which is respond to new terms of trade, respond to new incentives in the market," Greer said. "We're actually seeing a lot come back to North America."
Greer's comments also provided new detail from the U.S. side following Trump's meeting with Xi at the White House on Thursday. Beijing has so far released a more detailed public account of the talks than Washington.
Xi told Trump on Thursday that artificial intelligence presents greater opportunities for U.S.-China cooperation than competition, according to a Chinese state media readout.
"The two sides can continue AI dialogue, exchange views on risks and benefits, and together guard against the misuse or malicious use of AI," Xi said, according to a CNBC translation of the readout .
Trump, in a Truth Social post Friday morning, called the meeting with Xi "very productive" and said the Chinese leader appeared receptive to Trump's preferred term of "SUPER INTELLIGENCE" for artificial intelligence.
"Tremendous things will be happening," Trump wrote.

U.S. Treasury yields inched higher on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Fed commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up more than 2 basis points to 5.183% after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was higher by more than 1 basis point at 5.476% after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.901%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors weighed a global bond selloff this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
On Friday, the Commerce Department reported that durable goods orders in August were relatively unchanged. Economists polled by Dow Jones had expected a decline of 0.3%.
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."

articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift issues brutal warning about toxic ex in scathing ‘Patient Zero’ lyrics
articles.content_orig:
Taylor Swift’s latest lyrics are better than revenge.
The pop star issued a brutal warning about a toxic ex in her new song “Patient Zero” — and fans believe she was referring to former flame Joe Jonas, despite the singer claiming it was inspired by a friend’s situation.
In the new track off “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore,” out Friday, Swift sings about befriending her ex’s new girlfriend.
She describes herself as “patient zero” — meaning she was the first to experience the emotional damage caused by the unnamed partner’s love and manipulation — and recalls the new girlfriend confiding in her about the couple’s issues.
“If you wanna party with somebody who might know / About the devil on his shoulder under his halo / When the toxins take their hold, you’d rather die than let it go / But if you’re sick of him, I got you, I was patient zero,” she sings.
Many Swifties took to social media to claim the situation was reminiscent to Swift’s real-life dynamic with Joe Jonas and his now-ex-wife, Sophie Turner.
The Grammy winner briefly dated Jonas in 2008 before he, infamously, dumped her in a 27-second phone call.
Jonas began dating Turner in 2016, and in 2019, she and Swift seemed to become friendly, making several public appearances together.
However, it was the “Game of Thrones” alum’s 2023 separation from Jonas that brought her and the songwriter especially close.
Swift, notably, offered Turner her New York City apartment as a free, safe space for the actress and her two daughters during her custody and divorce battle with Jonas.
Due to this situation, many Swifties shared their theory that Swift believes she was Jonas’ “patient zero” and ultimately supported Turner because of it.
“so my patient zero theory is that she wrote this song for Sophie Turner amidst her very public divorce with Joe Jonas,” one theorized on X . “Joe & Taylor were each other’s first public romances, making her ‘patient zero.’ She heard the rumors about their breakup, & wasn’t surprised when sophie called.”
“I mean Sophie literally moved into her house lol 💯 it’s Sophie/Joe,” another added .
A third wrote , “Probably not about this but patient zero REALLY reminds me of when she and sophie turner became thick as thieves when her and joe jonas broke up.”
Others, however, are convinced Swift is singing about Joe Alwyn, who Swift dated for more than six years .
Many fans came to this conclusion by comparing “Patient Zero” to other songs Swift previously wrote about the “Hamnet” star.
In her 2019 track “Cruel Summer” — widely believed to be about the beginning of their love story — Swift invoked imagery of a devilish guy she fell for in the song’s pre-chorus.
Similarly, the songwriter compared the subject of “Patient Zero” to an angelic-looking devil with the line about her knowing about “the devil on his shoulder under his halo.”
Additionally, her 2022 song “You’re Losing Me,” which is interpreted as being about the slow breakdown of her relationship with the British actor, also featured a medical theme like “Patient Zero,” with a pulse in the background of the track.
Swift, however, shared the song’s inspiration with Capital FM on Friday, saying, “I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy.
“Everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, ‘Oh, I’ve been through that too’, and telling the stories of when this kind of reach out had happened for them,” she continued.
Reps for Swift, Jonas and Alwyn did not immediately respond to Page Six’s requests for comment.

articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long been set on owning the hardware that consumers use to access his company's apps. As he pushes to make the Muse AI agent the "centerpiece" of Meta's AI strategy, he's counting on a slew of forthcoming devices to turn his dream into reality.
At Meta's annual Connect conference, which landed a week before OpenAI's big event for developers, the company said that by the end of 2026, "there will be over 100 styles of AI glasses," and Zuckerberg on Wednesday revealed a pendant called the Muse Charm, though he didn't offer a price.
Meta was late to the generative AI game, badly trailing OpenAI , Anthropic and Google , which all have popular AI models and a host of services used by consumers and businesses. Zuckerberg is trying to make up for lost time with Muse, an app that can act as a personal assistant, responding to emails, booking travel and shopping on a user's behalf.
Investors are buying in, lifting the stock 4.5% on Thursday and more than 25% since Meta announced Muse earlier this month. They're betting that, while Zuckerberg never found a big market for virtual reality after changing his company's name to Meta five years ago and shifting its strategy to the metaverse, he's now on the right track.
"Meta Connect 2026 more explicitly attached Muse AI as a killer app fused deeply into the hardware strategy, from AR glasses and extending into Muse Charm, a dedicated keychain-like device providing rapid access to Muse," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report on Thursday. The firm, which recommends buying the stock, said Meta's AI advancements will continue "to drive multiple expansion in Meta shares."
The Muse Charm resembles a cross between a kid's Tamagotchi keychain and a wearable medical buzzer. Zuckerberg said Meta still needs to finalize the "finishing material" and "laying out the components" to have it ready to ship for the holidays.
As ChatGPT creator OpenAI gears up for its DevDay conference next week, anticipation has been building that Sam Altman's company may show off its long-awaited hardware product, which will reportedly be a hockey puck-like speaker .
OpenAI didn't respond to a request for comment.
In getting out ahead of OpenAI, Zuckerberg is building on the momentum of Muse, which skyrocketed to the top of Apple's App Store, eclipsing ChatGPT. Meanwhile, OpenAI and Anthropic are dealing with intensifying concerns about their market-leading AI models, as critics and company execs sound the alarm about potential harms to humanity.
For Zuckerberg, the Muse Charm is just his latest hardware endeavor as he tries to end his company's reliance on Apple for distribution. It's been a particularly sticky matter since Apple changed its privacy policy in 2021, limiting the ability for app developers to target users with adds.
Meta has found some success in smart glasses through a partnership with Ray-Ban parent EssilorLuxottica . The company said Wednesday that in the coming months it will be bringing Muse to its smart glasses, offering "hands-free access, activated by saying your agent's name."
Meta also unveiled Meta VR Glasses , which are slimmer and lighter than the older Quest-branded VR headsets, but are also more expensive, costing $1,299 when they go on sale next year. It's Meta's first VR device since 2024, when the company debuted the $299 Quest 3S.
The pendant represents an entirely new device category, but many experts say there's no clear sense of market demand given the ubiquity and capability of smartphones. Zuckerberg said it will contain a fingerprint sensor that, when activated, lets people talk to their AI agent.
"Why would I carry another device?" said Anthony Ferry, CEO of the e-commerce company Wayvia, in an interview after watching the Connect presentation. For it to be valuable, it has to be "easier than using my phone," he said, adding that, "If I still have to pull out my phone to finish the job or fix the order, it's just another thing to charge."
Anshika Jain, an analyst at Counterpoint Research, said she can see the appeal.
"Meta's Muse Charm reflects a broader shift in how consumers may interact with AI in real time, with a more convenient and simpler interface for everyday life," Jain said in an email. "At the core is the Muse AI agent, which is designed to understand context and take actions in a faster way rather than just responding to queries."
Jain said the Muse Charm could find "use cases such as asking questions, getting reminders, planning or accessing information while on the go."
In addition to proving that the sudden emergence of Muse isn't just a passing fad, Zuckerberg also has to find a workable economic model for the AI agent. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse from scanning its site to shop on behalf of customers, following similar moves against Perplexity, OpenAI and Google.
Zuckerberg said he expects that "over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions."
Ferry said companies will "need to look at whether this is actually growing their business," and not merely benefiting Meta's bottom line.
"If it brings you a customer you wouldn't have reached, great," Ferry said. "But if the same customer buys the same product through another channel, that isn't automatically a new sale. You have to understand what it costs and whether you're getting additional business for that money."
Ralph Schackart, an analyst at William Blair, wrote in a report  Thursday that, "Meta outlined a clear monetization framework, with the company expecting to generate revenue primarily by taking a small fee on transactions completed through Muse while keeping the product free for most users."

Joe Giudice is asking the public to have compassion for his daughter Milania Giudice after her recent airport incident.
In an exclusive statement to Page Six, the former “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star revealed Milania, 20, has been struggling privately with the loss of a close friend and the pressures of growing up in the public eye.
“Milania is a good girl. She has a big heart, she loves deeply, and she cares enormously about the people in her life,” Joe, 54, said. “She is also young and going through a very difficult period right now.”
Joe said the death of Milania’s close friend Victoria Zardoya in July “affected” his daughter “tremendously,” adding that she has been trying to process the loss while dealing with life in the spotlight.
“Losing someone you love is incredibly painful, and grief does not have a timeline,” he said. “She has been trying to process that loss while also dealing with the pressures that come with growing up in the public eye.”
Joe also cautioned against judging Milania based on a single moment, saying, “I know my daughter. I know her heart, and I know that what people may see from the outside does not tell the whole story of what someone is experiencing privately.
“There have been difficult moments, but those moments do not define who Milania is as a person.”
Joe, who is represented by Dominton Talent House, added, “I love my daughter, and I will always stand beside her.”
His comments come after Milania was captured in a since-deleted video getting into a heated exchange with her mother, Teresa Giudice, 54, and older sister, Gia Giudice, 25, at an airport while surrounded by police.
In the clip, Milania repeatedly asked, “This is what we do now?” as Teresa told her, “I love you.” Gia then told her mother to “let her do what she wants to do” before Milania snapped at Teresa, saying “Shut the f–k up!”
The video offered little context for what prompted the confrontation, but an incident report obtained by Page Six explained that Milania was “having suicidal thoughts” and a “mental breakdown” at Tampa International Airport in Florida on Wednesday.
Cops were notified that “multiple females need police ASAP,” that Milania “got away” from her family and that she had been separated from a counselor who was traveling with them.
Milania was located about 10 minutes later and was escorted to her gate by police. There was no arrest or medical transport.

Milania had just been “released” from a nearby hospital, according to law enforcement sources who spoke to US Sun .
The airport incident came after Milania was arrested in New Jersey on a simple assault charge stemming from a domestic dispute at her mother’s home on May 14.
According to a police report, Milania was “throwing food [and] candles” during the dispute, while her sister Gabriella Giudice called 911 and reported that she was “acting erratically.” No weapons or injuries were reported. A judge later alleged during Milania’s arraignment that she struck the alleged victim , identified only as “LR,” in the head with her fist, causing redness to the person’s forehead. Milania pleaded not guilty.
She subsequently enrolled in anger management classes as part of the ongoing case. In August, her attorney told a judge they were postponing her hearing so she could complete the course.
For Joe, however, the focus is supporting his daughter as she works through what he described as an especially painful chapter.
“As her father, my priority is making sure my daughter knows that she is loved and supported,” he said. “Our family is doing everything we can to be there for her and give her the support and space she needs right now.”

The New York City Council is readying legislation to rein in the artificial intelligence industry as AI companies continue to grow their presence in the city.
One bill will ban businesses from selling or deploying AI systems in the city unless an independent inspector certified they met city standards for data quality, bias, privacy and security, Fortune reported Friday morning.
That bill will also require AI labs to engineer a "kill switch," i.e. a human override to shut down a model or agent in the event it goes rogue.
Failing to comply with these regulations will lead to $25,000 fines per violation, City Council Speaker Julie Menin told Fortune in an interview. Since the penalties would be assessed for each AI agent involved, the total fines could be substantial.
Another piece of legislation will reward whistleblowers with a portion of the fines collected from AI firms who break the law, Fortune reported.
The new regulations are expected to be introduced on Friday ahead of an Oct. 5 Committee of the Whole hearing with all 51 council members in attendance.
Pope Leo XIV warned Friday that a "paradise of machines" could pose a risk to humanity during the opening to his four-day trip in France .
In a speech at the Élysée Palace, the pope said it was an urgent concern of his that "we do not lose our humanity amid the paradise of machines that are invading and conditioning our daily lives," according to the Guardian.
The phrase "paradise of machines" is a reference to Georges Bernanos’s 1947 essay "France Against the Robots," in which he argued that industrialization and technological advancement was contributing to the dulling of the human spirit and mass loneliness.
Pope Leo has made artificial intelligence one of the defining issues of his papacy, creating a commission within the Vatican in May to address the growing ethical concerns with AI.
"Technology should not be considered, in itself, as a force antagonistic to humanity," Pope Leo wrote in his May 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. "At the same time, each phase of progress has also revealed the ambiguity of tools that can cause harm when not oriented toward the good."
A federal appeals court ruled Friday that the Trump administration is allowed to exclude Anthropic from being considered for all U.S. military contracts.
In a 2-1 ruling, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Pentagon acted lawfully when it removed Anthropic's Claude AI from its supply chain.
The court argued that the company's ability to restrict how its models performed on certain "lawful" military tasks constituted a national security risk under federal law.
Back in February, the Pentagon claimed Anthropic had asked whether its product was used in the January military operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Fox News Digital reported at the time.
Sources told Fox News Digital that Anthropic posed this question in a way that suggested it may not approve of its potential involvement in the Maduro operation.
The relationship between the Department of War and Anthropic deteriorated further when CEO Dario Amodei put out a blog post on Feb. 26, saying he would not allow Claude to be used for "mass domestic surveillance" or "fully autonomous weapons."
"Anthropic understands that the Department of War, not private companies, makes military decisions," Amodei wrote. "However, in a narrow set of cases, we believe AI can undermine, rather than defend, democratic values."
Shortly after Amodei's statement was released, War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the federal government would cease using all of Anthropic's technology.
"Our position has never wavered and will never waver: the Department of War must have full, unrestricted access to Anthropic’s models for every LAWFUL purpose in defense of the Republic," Hegseth wrote in a post on X at the time. "Cloaked in the sanctimonious rhetoric of 'effective altruism,' they have attempted to strong-arm the United States military into submission."
Jason Calacanis, an angel investor and Dotcom era startup founder, put out a cryptic social media post advising SpaceX and Meta to release "an iPhone competitor with no apps — just agents and optimized for local AI and privacy."
His post on X included a screenshot of an iPhone dock showing just two apps: xAI's Grok Bot and Meta's Muse, two advanced AI agent systems designed to automate complex work tasks.
It's not entirely clear what Calacanis is envisioning, but Meta has already waded into introducing hardware paired with its AI software.
This week, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced the Muse Charm, a pocket-watch-sized device that would have the Muse AI agent system included.
"We packed the whole Muse experience, including the whole real-time voice and avatar stack, into something that fits on a keychain and is always available to talk to," Zuckerberg said at this year's Meta Connect event.
If the gadget were to catch on, users would not need to access Muse via a smartphone from Apple or Google, potentially cutting into those companies' profit margins. The Muse Charm is expected to roll out sometime in December.
Pope Leo XIV’s cardinal who leads an artificial intelligence commission within the Vatican admitted on a Politico podcast that he doesn't use AI.
Cardinal Michael Czerny told the Brussels Playbook Podcast that he hasn't had the time to start using it in his daily work, even though the pope appointed him to chair the Vatican’s Inter-Dicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence four months ago.
“I’m quite willing and happy to learn,” Czerny said. “I feel it’s my moral duty also to use it so that I have personal experience, and I hope it helps me with my work.”
Czerny has called on European politicians to heed warnings about frontier AI models breaking free of human oversight.
Chinese AI startup DeepSeek has hit an annualized revenue run rate of $1 billion, more than double what it was a few months ago, The Information reported.
An annualized revenue run rate estimates how much money a company would make in a year if it continued earning at its current pace.
DeepSeek stunned Silicon Valley last year when its AI models proved competitive with leading offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic, despite being developed with far fewer resources.
Reuters reported earlier this month that DeepSeek is planning to go public domestically to fund its expansion.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Wednesday that companies developing advanced artificial intelligence models do not need to work together to prevent the catastrophic outcomes that many industry leaders have warned about.
In an interview with former Wall Street Journal columnist Joanna Stern, Zuckerberg also cast doubt on the mores alarmist members of the AI sector, some of whom have said human extinction is possibility if AI improves without guardrails in place.
"I think that there's a lot of rhetoric that is filled with doom, and my view on this is that there are a number of labs that are working on building advanced AI, and I don't think that we need some kind of  industry-wide coordination to not necessarily mess this up," he said on Stern's show "New Things."
"I think that just each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to make sure that you're proceeding safely," Zuckerberg added.
Meta launched its personal AI assistant, Muse, on Sept. 8 in the United States. It's available on major app stores and has been integrated into Meta's Ray Ban audio glasses.

“The amount of compute in space will obviously round up to 100% of all compute,” Musk wrote on X in response to a video about Google’s Project Suncatcher.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed allegations that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza as “the biggest lie of the century” during a defiant address to the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday, as scores of delegates walked out in protest.
“Here's the simple truth. Israel didn't commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide,” Netanyahu said, calling the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) “the most moral army in the world.” He pointed to Israel’s facilitation of food aid and polio vaccination campaigns in Gaza, saying “Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way.”
Israel faces allegations of genocide in a case brought by South Africa before the International Court of Justice . The court has ordered Israel to take provisional measures under the Genocide Convention but has not ruled on whether Israel has committed genocide. The case remains pending.
In September 2025, an independent U.N. commission of inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide, and the International Association of Genocide Scholars said Israel’s policies and actions met the legal definition of the crime. Israel has rejected the findings.
Netanyahu sharply criticized New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani during his speech, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and placing him among “all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers.”
“Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York,” Netanyahu said. He reiterated his claims that the mayor supports Hamas and has “ incit[ed] riots against New York Jews .” Mamdani has denied supporting Hamas. “Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can’t silence me and you can’t silence the truth,” Netanyahu said.
In response to Netanyahu’s remarks, Mamdani accused the Israeli leader of using his speech to “repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”
“Yet no lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity,” Mandani said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s remarks come amid heightened concern about antisemitism in New York, where anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 57% of all reported hate crimes in 2025, according to NYPD data . Mamdani has rejected accusations of antisemitism and proposed increasing the city’s hate-crime prevention budget from $3 million to $26 million. His administration has also maintained a dedicated Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism .
The dispute stretches back to Mamdani’s mayoral campaign. A longtime critic of Israel’s military actions in Gaza, Mamdani has repeatedly condemned Netanyahu, calling him “a war criminal and an architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people.” He also vowed to have Netanyahu arrested under an International Criminal Court warrant issued over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Mamdani later acknowledged that the city lacked the independent authority to execute the warrant and called on the federal government to arrest Netanyahu instead.
Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump, saying Israel has “no greater partner.” He pointed to the joint U.S.-Israeli operation that he said had destroyed much of Iran’s nuclear program after the two countries launched their war against Iran in February. He called attacking Iran “one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as Prime Minister.”
Netanyahu also accused Qatar of spending billions of dollars to finance universities and the Al Jazeera media network as part of an effort to “brainwash young minds to hate Israel, America and the West.” He also criticized the country for hosting Hamas leaders. Netanyahu went on to accuse Turkey of being a “super-spreader of antisemitic lies” and condemned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for also hosting Hamas leaders. Turkey and Qatar are yet to respond to the statement.
Outside the United Nations, several hundred protesters gathered with chants of "stop arming Israel, let Gaza live" and "stop arming Israel, let Iran live" ahead of Netanyahu’s speech.

In a prerecorded address shown at the U.N. General Assembly earlier Thursday, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas said that “the Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times of its history.”
“How much longer will some states continue to remain silent on Israel or supply it with the weapons that it uses against our people?” Abbas said. He accused Israel of “ethnic cleansing” and a “genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.”
The U.S. denied Abbas and other Palestinian officials visas to attend the assembly in person for the second consecutive year, accusing the Palestinian Authority of “glorifying terrorism.” Abbas condemned what he called the “unlawful punitive measures” and called on the Trump administration to lift the restrictions on his delegation and on the U.N. to grant Palestine “full membership” in the international organization. He also called for the State of Palestine to be granted full U.N. membership.
According to the Gaza Health Ministry, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas terror attack on Oct. 7, 2023 , which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and saw about 250 others taken hostage.
Since the ceasefire was signed in October 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed according to the ministry. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. Data from the IDF suggests a Palestinian civilian death rate of 83% .
The U.N. in October estimated that Gaza required $70 billion to reverse the damage caused by two years of war to its infrastructure.
The war in Gaza has been a major focus for world leaders addressing the U.N. in New York this week.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres , whose nearly decade-long tenure leading the international body comes to an end at the start of next year, said during his address on Tuesday that Gaza has experienced “a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General.” He added that Israel’s “violence, displacement and settlement expansion” raised the “specter of ethnic cleansing.”
Trump said the war in Gaza was over . He took credit for ending it, “saving untold thousands of lives,” and brokering the return of the remaining hostages held in Gaza. But key elements of the peace agreement Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’ disarmament, a long-term plan for governing Gaza, and the delivery of humanitarian aid—remain largely stalled.

U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Federal Reserve commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up more than 4 basis points to 5.209% after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was higher by more than 5 basis points at 5.516% after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.897%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors also weighed a global bond sell-off this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
On Friday, durable goods orders in August came in relatively unchanged , while economists polled by Dow Jones had expected a decline of 0.3%. Additionally, consumer sentiment plummeted in September.

The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif in western Saudi ​Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, with the Houthis claiming their attacks were aimed at “a sensitive target” in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Oil prices climbed about 3%, but trade was volatile and prices came off session highs after reports the US and Iran discussed reopening the strait of Hormuz .
The escalating attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s ⁠ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the strait of Hormuz is disrupted and the kingdom’s east-west pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier ​this month . The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a ‌second theatre in the US-Iran war.
It was ‌not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil.
The Houthis seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government pressed world leaders on Thursday for help defeating the militants, saying that their new perch along one of the world’s busiest waterways presents an international economic risk.
While claiming that their blockade only applies to Saudi shipping and there remains no threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, the Houths have also warned other nations not to get involved.
But the vice-president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN general assembly not to trust the Houthis’ assurances – and to see a bigger picture in the crisis around the strait.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” said vice-president, Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer.
Arguing that protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” he urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels’ hands.
The Saudi-backed government’s forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen’s third-biggest city Taiz from the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, government sources said.
The Houthis ⁠have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the ​only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel ​abroad. Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to ​tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.
Riyadh’s foreign ministry said on Friday that Saudi ⁠Arabia, Turkey and ⁠Pakistan would ⁠hold ​an urgent ⁠meeting of their chiefs ⁠of ​staff ‌to ‌discuss ways to ‌support repel the Houthi attacks under their joint ‌defence agreement. Under the defence pact, all three countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Officials in Pakistan are said to be deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East.

articles.title_orig: Trump lavishes China's Xi during state visit. What did the summit accomplish?
articles.title_zh: Trump lavishes China's Xi during state visit. What did the summit accomplish?

During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.
Mr. Trump did not answer shouted questions about Taiwan, Iran or whether Mr. Trump asked Xi to free imprisoned pro-democracy Hong Kong media tycoon Jimmy Lai .
A group of demonstrators was audible from the White House's North Portico ahead of Thursday evening's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
A woman with a megaphone led a crowd of protesters through chants like: "Xi Jinping, You're Not Welcome," "Free Hong Kong," "Keep Taiwan Free" and "China Sponsors Genocide."
Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, have arrived at the White House state dinner.
Several minutes later, fellow tech titan Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, walked into the event.
Other high-profile executives are expected to attend the dinner, including the CEOs of Nvidia, Qualcomm and OpenAI, CBS News has previously reported.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis questioned President Trump's judgment in hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state dinner at the White House this week, saying he's "worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations."
"It's a WTF moment," the retiring North Carolina senator said in an interview with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil on Thursday about Mr. Trump's red-carpet rollout for Xi compared to the reception that some U.S. allies like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have received.
"It's not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation. Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview," he said.
President Trump took to Truth Social to voice his frustration that CNN and MS NOW didn't air the arrival ceremony for Xi, saying it was "made for television." Other networks, including CBS News, also didn't air the arrival ceremony.
CNN and MS NOW, along with Politico, were banned from the White House last week. While a federal judge ordered the outlets' access to be restored, it's not clear whether CNN will be allowed to participate in the White House television pool . And as long as CNN lacks a guarantee that it will be in the regular pool rotation again, the other four networks that make up the pool also aren't participating.
Members of the pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — are declining to provide video coverage of the president until the White House guarantees it will let CNN back in. Some networks chose not to air the government's feed of the event, since the television pool was not present. News outlets are still reporting on the event itself.
The arrival ceremony for Xi was not open to all media, but only to the pool. ABC News was the representative for the pool on Thursday.
"CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng," Mr. Trump wrote.
